Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Sequence Continuation: Analyzing Shared Circuits in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models re-use shared circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, such as Arabic numerals, number words, and months.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that large language models re-use shared sub-circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, and shows that these circuits have analogous functionality across different models like GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformers leverage shared computational structures across similar tasks, advancing the understanding of how they represent abstract concepts and contributing to mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Shared sub-circuits exist for similar sequence continuation tasks in both GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B.
Key components include attention heads for sequence member detection (e.g., head 4.4) and successor prediction (e.g., head 9.1), as well as MLP 9 for next member calculation.
These circuits affect a wide range of math-related prompts, including intervaled sequences and arithmetic tasks.
The functionality of components is consistent across tasks, indicating re-use of computational structures.
Analogous sub-circuits are found in different models, suggesting common mechanisms for sequence processing.
future_direction: Examine if shared circuits appear in more models
Expand studies on non-linear features and their effects on math-related circuits
papers.abstract: While transformer models exhibit strong capabilities on linguistic tasks, their complex architectures make them difficult to interpret. Recent work has aimed to reverse engineer transformer models into human-readable representations called circuits that implement algorithmic functions. We extend this research by analyzing and comparing circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, which include increasing sequences of Arabic numerals, number words, and months. By applying circuit interpretability analysis, we identify a key sub-circuit in both GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B responsible for detecting sequence members and for predicting the next member in a sequence. Our analysis reveals that semantically related sequences rely on shared circuit subgraphs with analogous roles. Additionally, we show that this sub-circuit has effects on various math-related prompts, such as on intervaled circuits, Spanish number word and months continuation, and natural language word problems. Overall, documenting shared computational structures enables better model behavior predictions, identification of errors, and safer editing procedures. This mechanistic understanding of transformers is a critical step towards building more robust, aligned, and interpretable language models.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Analyzing analytical methods: The case of phonology in neural models of spoken language
papers.research_question: How do diagnostic classifiers and representational similarity analysis compare in analyzing neural representations of phonology, and how do factors like learning (trained vs random) and temporal scope (local vs global) affect the outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reporting analysis results with randomly initialized models is crucial, and that global-scope methods tend to yield more consistent results, recommending their use as a complement to local-scope diagnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: The study recommends using global methods as a complement to local diagnostic methods and always including randomly initialized models as a baseline in representational analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Local RSA shows low correlations and does not separate trained vs random models well.
Global methods (both diagnostic and RSA) are more sensitive to learning and show consistent results across layers.
Randomly initialized RNNs encode phoneme information in higher layers due to recurrent connectivity, while random Transformers do not.
The impact of learning is more salient with global representations than local ones.
Attention-based pooling is more erratic and harder to optimize than mean pooling.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to completely control for the many factors of variation in target models due to architectural modifications required by different objectives and datasets.
future_direction: Sample target models with a larger number of plausible combinations of factors.
Further disentangle differences between analytical methods.
papers.abstract: Given the fast development of analysis techniques for NLP and speech processing systems, few systematic studies have been conducted to compare the strengths and weaknesses of each method. As a step in this direction we study the case of representations of phonology in neural network models of spoken language. We use two commonly applied analytical techniques, diagnostic classifiers and representational similarity analysis, to quantify to what extent neural activation patterns encode phonemes and phoneme sequences. We manipulate two factors that can affect the outcome of analysis. First, we investigate the role of learning by comparing neural activations extracted from trained versus randomly-initialized models. Second, we examine the temporal scope of the activations by probing both local activations corresponding to a few milliseconds of the speech signal, and global activations pooled over the whole utterance. We conclude that reporting analysis results with randomly initialized models is crucial, and that global-scope methods tend to yield more consistent results and we recommend their use as a complement to local-scope diagnostic methods.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Do Transformers know symbolic rules, and would we know if they did?
papers.research_question: Do Transformers internalize genuine symbolic rules, and how can we distinguish symbolic rule use from associative pattern matching?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that Transformers may function as the processor component within a larger symbolic architecture that uses input and output as external memory, and experimentally shows that generalization for abstract rules is significantly stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in classification tasks.
papers.conclusion: The question of whether Transformers internalize symbolic rules remains open, but the full input-Transformer-output pipeline can satisfy the architectural criterion of symbolicity by using attention and positional encoding for location-based memory addressing.
papers.key_findings:
T5 demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization across vocabularies in all tested tasks.
In vocabulary flip settings, T5 completely fails at classification tasks without data mixing, but achieves moderate success in sequence-to-sequence tasks even without mixing.
Repetition detection remains difficult for T5 even with mixed data, indicating a specific obstacle to learning abstract rules when associative heuristics are unavailable.
Generalization is systematically stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in comparable classification tasks.
The results highlight the challenge of conclusively attributing symbolic rule internalization to Transformers due to the unfalsifiability of non-symbolic explanations.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup is simple and artificial, using artificial vocabularies of single characters and restricting the model architecture to T5.
The classification tasks are restricted to binary targets, and experiments are limited to a single Transformer variant.
future_direction: Examine the performance of tokens with more prevalent linguistic functions and compare different linguistic classes and languages in multilingual models.
Expand experiments to multi-class and multi-label settings, and to more Transformer variants and hyperparameters.
Investigate whether non-symbolic associative explanations for zero-shot success on identical token detection are plausible in practice.
papers.abstract: To improve the explainability of leading Transformer networks used in NLP, it is important to tease apart genuine symbolic rules from merely associative input-output patterns. However, we identify several inconsistencies in how ``symbolicity'' has been construed in recent NLP literature. To mitigate this problem, we propose two criteria to be the most relevant, one pertaining to a system's internal architecture and the other to the dissociation between abstract rules and specific input identities. From this perspective, we critically examine prior work on the symbolic capacities of Transformers, and deem the results to be fundamentally inconclusive for reasons inherent in experiment design. We further maintain that there is no simple fix to this problem, since it arises -- to an extent -- in all end-to-end settings. Nonetheless, we emphasize the need for more robust evaluation of whether non-symbolic explanations exist for success in seemingly symbolic tasks. To facilitate this, we experiment on four sequence modelling tasks on the T5 Transformer in two experiment settings: zero-shot generalization, and generalization across class-specific vocabularies flipped between the training and test set. We observe that T5's generalization is markedly stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in comparable classification tasks. Based on this, we propose a thus far overlooked analysis, where the Transformer itself does not need to be symbolic to be part of a symbolic architecture as the processor, operating on the input and output as external memory components.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Anatomy of an Idiom: Tracing Non-Compositionality in Language Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms do transformers use to process and make sense of natural language, specifically focusing on the processing of non-compositional idiomatic expressions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a modified path patching algorithm for circuit discovery and uses it to identify specialized 'Idiom Heads' and a mechanism called 'augmented reception' in transformer models processing idioms, revealing how they balance computational efficiency and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that transformers process idioms in early layers with a sequential structure, identify specialized Idiom Heads, and reveal augmented reception as a mechanism for efficient attention, providing insights into non-compositional language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Idioms acquire their non-compositional (figurative) meaning in early layers (0-5) of the network, with a two-phase structure: cross-token attention in layers 0-2 followed by semantic integration in layers 3-5.
Specific attention heads ('Idiom Heads') consistently activate across multiple idioms, suggesting functional specialization for non-compositional language processing.
Each idiom employs a distinct direction in Query-Key space rather than a universal 'idiom direction'.
Early processing of idiom tokens creates 'augmented reception,' enhancing the receptivity of later attention heads to idiom-specific tokens, which is a mechanism for efficient attention allocation.
Most idiomatic processing occurs on the final token of the expression, deferring computation until all necessary context is available.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English idioms in a single model architecture (Gemma 2–2B).
Threshold determination for circuit discovery introduces subjective elements.
future_direction: Broader study of more idioms in multiple languages and transformer models to confirm generality.
Investigate whether similar patterns occur for other non-compositional phenomena, like grammatical constructions.
Further examples and investigation into augmented reception to deepen understanding of transformer information processing.
papers.abstract: We investigate the processing of idiomatic expressions in transformer-based language models using a novel set of techniques for circuit discovery and analysis. First discovering circuits via a modified path patching algorithm, we find that idiom processing exhibits distinct computational patterns. We identify and investigate ``Idiom Heads,'' attention heads that frequently activate across different idioms, as well as enhanced attention between idiom tokens due to earlier processing, which we term ``augmented reception.'' We analyze these phenomena and the general features of the discovered circuits as mechanisms by which transformers balance computational efficiency and robustness. Finally, these findings provide insights into how transformers handle non-compositional language and suggest pathways for understanding the processing of more complex grammatical constructions.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models perform multi-step reasoning? The paper aims to uncover the reasoning mechanisms (thought processes) used by language models in complex reasoning tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF), which combines circuit analysis and self-influence functions to trace and analyze the reasoning pathways of language models, demonstrating its application on GPT-2 for the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that SICAF successfully maps reasoning pathways in language models, revealing a hierarchical reasoning structure similar to human thought processes.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace the thought process of language models during complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified by EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL are more faithful and compact than those identified by EAP.
The model's key parameters are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The reasoning process follows a hierarchical structure: early layers identify entities, middle layers interpret actions, and final layers synthesize information.
Self-influence scores show how token importance changes across layers, revealing the reasoning path.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
Our work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of this approach across varied tasks and model architectures
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved significant success; however, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque due to the complexity of non-linear interactions and high-dimensional operations. While previous studies have demonstrated that these models implicitly embed reasoning trees, humans typically employ various distinct logical reasoning mechanisms to complete the same task. It is still unclear which multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve such tasks. In this paper, we aim to address this question by investigating the mechanistic interpretability of language models, particularly in the context of multi-step reasoning tasks. Specifically, we employ circuit analysis and self-influence functions to evaluate the changing importance of each token throughout the reasoning process, allowing us to map the reasoning paths adopted by the model. We apply this methodology to the GPT-2 model on a prediction task (IOI) and demonstrate that the underlying circuits reveal a human-interpretable reasoning process used by the model.

papers.title: Abstraction in time: Finding hierarchical linguistic structure in a model of relational processing
papers.research_question: Does the oscillatory activation in LISA/DORA models during processing match human cortical activity during language processing, suggesting a common mechanism for hierarchical representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LISA/DORA models of relational processing exhibit oscillatory activation patterns during sentence processing that closely match human cortical tracking of hierarchical linguistic structures, suggesting that mechanisms for relational binding may underlie language representation.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that abstract hierarchical linguistic representations can be processed by models of relational reasoning, and suggests that integrating such models with language processing models could advance cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LISA/DORA models parse English sentences and show firing patterns that mirror cortical activity observed in Ding et al. (2016), with activation bursts at sentence (1Hz), phrasal (2Hz), and syllabic (4Hz) rates.
The models' binding mechanisms, using temporal synchrony and asynchrony, naturally produce hierarchical representations similar to those in human language processing.
These models, built for analogy and relational learning, generalize to language processing without modification, unlike grammar-based or statistical models.
The results support the idea that relational role representation may be a foundation for human cognitive capacities like language.
Integrating models of relational reasoning and language processing could lead to more plausible cognitive models.
future_direction: Testing on natural speech input
Testing on varied syntactic structures
Testing in rich discourse contexts and multilingual input
papers.abstract: Abstract mental representation is fundamental for human cognition. Forming such representations in time, especially from dynamic and noisy perceptual input, is a challenge for any processing modality, but perhaps none so acutely as for language processing. We show that LISA (Hummel & Holyaok, 1997) and DORA (Doumas, Hummel, & Sandhofer, 2008), models built to process and to learn structured (i.e., symbolic) rep resentations of conceptual properties and relations from unstructured inputs, show oscillatory activation during processing that is highly similar to the cortical activity elicited by the linguistic stimuli from Ding et al.(2016). We argue, as Ding et al.(2016), that this activation reflects formation of hierarchical linguistic representation, and furthermore, that the kind of computational mechanisms in LISA/DORA (e.g., temporal binding by systematic asynchrony of firing) may underlie formation of abstract linguistic representations in the human brain. It may be this repurposing that allowed for the generation or mergence of hierarchical linguistic structure, and therefore, human language, from extant cognitive and neural systems. We conclude that models of thinking and reasoning and models of language processing must be integrated —not only for increased plausiblity, but in order to advance both fields towards a larger integrative model of human cognition

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Unveiling Language Competence Neurons: A Psycholinguistic Approach to Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do language models capture deeper cognitive aspects of language competence, and can specific neurons be identified that correspond to such competence?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that in GPT-2-XL, human-like language competence in psycholinguistic tasks is supported by specific neurons, as evidenced by ablation and activation experiments; tasks where the model lacks competence show no such neuron specialization.
papers.conclusion: Psycholinguistic tasks offer a powerful framework for probing neuron-level representations in language models, linking language abilities to specific neurons and providing insights into how LLMs process language.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2-XL does not exhibit human-like sound-shape association, and neuron manipulation does not affect performance on this task.
GPT-2-XL shows marginal human-like sound-gender association, and neuron manipulation (ablation and activation) affects performance, indicating specific neurons are involved.
GPT-2-XL shows strong human-like implicit causality understanding, and neuron manipulation strongly affects performance, indicating specific neurons are crucial.
The top 5 and top 50 neurons identified by accumulative direct effect are causally important for tasks where the model exhibits competence.
Psycholinguistic tasks can be used to probe neuron-level representations in language models, linking language abilities to specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
Use of GPT-2-XL, an older and smaller model, which may not generalize to newer models.
Focus on only three psycholinguistic tasks, which provides a narrow view of language competence.
Granularity of neuron manipulation techniques may overlook distributed representations.
future_direction: Extend these methods to more advanced models.
Explore additional psycholinguistic phenomena.
Investigate other LLM architectures.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance in their linguistic capacity, understanding how they capture aspects of language competence remains a significant challenge. This study therefore employs psycholinguistic paradigms in English, which are well-suited for probing deeper cognitive aspects of language processing, to explore neuron-level representations in language model across three tasks: sound-shape association, sound-gender association, and implicit causality. Our findings indicate that while GPT-2-XL struggles with the sound-shape task, it demonstrates human-like abilities in both sound-gender association and implicit causality. Targeted neuron ablation and activation manipulation reveal a crucial relationship: When GPT-2-XL displays a linguistic ability, specific neurons correspond to that competence; conversely, the absence of such an ability indicates a lack of specialized neurons. This study is the first to utilize psycholinguistic experiments to investigate deep language competence at the neuron level, providing a new level of granularity in model interpretability and insights into the internal mechanisms driving language ability in the transformer-based LLM.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: Towards Universality: Studying Mechanistic Similarity Across Language Model Architectures
papers.research_question: Does mechanistic understanding transfer across different model architectures? Specifically, how similar are the features and circuits in Transformer and Mamba models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer and Mamba models learn similar interpretable features as extracted by Sparse Autoencoders, and their induction circuits are structurally analogous, with a nuanced Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that SAE feature similarity is a useful measure for cross-architectural universality, revealing significant similarity between Transformer and Mamba features and circuits, with an Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE features in Pythia and Mamba are similar, with high Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation (MPPC).
Feature similarity is affected by semantic complexity; simpler features have higher correlation.
Induction circuits in Mamba are analogous to those in Transformers, but with an Off-by-One motif where information is written into the SSM state at the next token.
SAE features show depth specialization across architectures, with matched features appearing at proportionally similar layers.
The neuron baseline shows almost zero similarity, indicating SAEs are better for cross-architecture comparison than neuron-based methods.
papers.limitation:
SAEs may not capture all true features and might capture combinations of features rather than the features themselves.
Circuit universality analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative automated comparison tools.
future_direction: Automating circuit discovery and comparison for quantitative measurement of circuit universality.
Further study on the Off-by-One motif in Mamba circuits to understand its purpose and formation.
papers.abstract: The hypothesis of Universality in interpretability suggests that different neural networks may converge to implement similar algorithms on similar tasks. In this work, we investigate two mainstream architectures for language modeling, namely Transformers and Mambas, to explore the extent of their mechanistic similarity. We propose to use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to isolate interpretable features from these models and show that most features are similar in these two models. We also validate the correlation between feature similarity and Universality. We then delve into the circuit-level analysis of Mamba models and find that the induction circuits in Mamba are structurally analogous to those in Transformers. We also identify a nuanced difference we call \emph{Off-by-One motif}: The information of one token is written into the SSM state in its next position. Whilst interaction between tokens in Transformers does not exhibit such trend.

papers.title: Encoding of phonology in a recurrent neural model of grounded speech
papers.research_question: How is phonological information encoded in the layers of a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech, and how does the encoding change across layers with respect to form and meaning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how phoneme representations are encoded across layers of a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech, finding that phonological information is strongest in lower layers but persists in higher layers, and that the attention mechanism attenuates phonology to achieve semantic invariance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that phonological information is encoded most strongly in lower layers of the model, but persists in higher layers, and that the attention mechanism filters out phonological details to focus on semantic meaning.
papers.key_findings:
Phoneme representations are most salient in the lower layers of the model, where low-level signals are processed at a fine-grained level.
A large amount of phonological information is retained at the top recurrent layer.
The attention mechanism following the top recurrent layer significantly attenuates encoding of phonology and makes utterance embeddings more invariant to synonymy.
Hierarchical clustering of phoneme representations learned by the network shows an organizational structure similar to linguistic classifications.
The model can discriminate phonemes with high accuracy, and lower layers are more informative for this task than higher layers or input features.
papers.limitation: The model is trained on synthetic speech, which is easier to process than natural human-generated speech.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to grounded human speech to investigate whether context and speaker-invariant phoneme representations can be learned from natural, noisy input.
Compare the results to similar analyses applied to neuroimaging data.
papers.abstract: We study the representation and encoding of phonemes in a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech. We use a model which processes images and their spoken descriptions, and projects the visual and auditory representations into the same semantic space. We perform a number of analyses on how information about individual phonemes is encoded in the MFCC features extracted from the speech signal, and the activations of the layers of the model. Via experiments with phoneme decoding and phoneme discrimination we show that phoneme representations are most salient in the lower layers of the model, where low-level signals are processed at a fine-grained level, although a large amount of phonological information is retain at the top recurrent layer. We further find out that the attention mechanism following the top recurrent layer significantly attenuates encoding of phonology and makes the utterance embeddings much more invariant to synonymy. Moreover, a hierarchical clustering of phoneme representations learned by the network shows an organizational structure of phonemes similar to those proposed in linguistics.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Emergence of Phonemic, Syntactic, and Semantic Representations in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Whether and when phonemic, lexical and syntactic representations emerge in the activations of artificial neural networks during their training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that speech- and text-based models follow a sequence of learning stages where phonemic, lexical, and syntactic representations emerge in their activations, but require 2 to 4 orders of magnitude more data than children for these representations to emerge.
papers.conclusion: These results show conditions under which major stages of language acquisition spontaneously emerge in neural networks, delineating a promising path to understand the computations underpinning language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Phonemic structure, mirroring articulatory features, emerges in self-supervised speech models.
Lexical semantic structure (WordNet hypernymy) emerges in both text and speech models, but more strongly in text models.
Syntactic structure (dependency trees) emerges in both text and speech models.
The order of acquisition in audio models is phonemic, then partial lexical semantic, then syntactic.
Models require 2-4 orders of magnitude more data than children for these linguistic representations to emerge.
papers.limitation:
The models require 2 to 4 orders of magnitude more data than children for linguistic representations to emerge.
The semantic code only partially emerges in audio models, with scores potentially explained by acoustic correlates.
papers.abstract: During language acquisition, children successively learn to categorize phonemes, identify words, and combine them with syntax to form new meaning. While the development of this behavior is well characterized, we still lack a unifying computational framework to explain its underlying neural representations. Here, we investigate whether and when phonemic, lexical, and syntactic representations emerge in the activations of artificial neural networks during their training. Our results show that both speech- and text-based models follow a sequence of learning stages: during training, their neural activations successively build subspaces, where the geometry of the neural activations represents phonemic, lexical, and syntactic structure. While this developmental trajectory qualitatively relates to children's, it is quantitatively different: These algorithms indeed require two to four orders of magnitude more data for these neural representations to emerge. Together, these results show conditions under which major stages of language acquisition spontaneously emerge, and hence delineate a promising path to understand the computations underpinning language acquisition.

papers.title: An explainable transformer circuit for compositional generalization
papers.research_question: How does a compact transformer achieve compositional induction? What is the underlying circuit responsible for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and mechanistically interprets the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer, and shows that this understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can implement structured and interpretable mechanisms for compositional functions, and disassembling transformer circuitry yields benefits for understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of specific attention heads that implement compositional induction, including Output Head, Primitive-Pairing Head, Question-Broadcast Head, RHS-Scanner Head, Primitive-Retrieval Head, and Function-Retrieval Head.
Validated the circuit through causal ablations, showing how index information flows from question to output.
Demonstrated that swapping positional embeddings in the circuit leads to predictable changes in attention patterns, confirming the causal role of the circuit.
Provided a program-like description of the algorithm implemented by the transformer circuit.
Showed that the circuit encodes both index-in-question and relative-index-on-LHS information, which are matched in the Output Head's QK alignment.
papers.limitation:
The circuit analysis focused on a relatively small transformer; it is unclear if similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
The techniques required substantial human effort (path-patching, ablations, interpretation); for large-scale models, manual approaches become less feasible.
Targeted activation swaps only partially perturb the model's behavior due to the distributed nature of the mechanism; complete perturbation requires coordinating interventions across multiple heads.
future_direction: Investigating whether similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
Developing automated or semi-automated methods for circuit discovery and interpretation to reduce human effort.
Creating systematic workflows for coordinating interventions across all heads to achieve complete perturbation.
papers.abstract: Compositional generalization-the systematic combination of known components into novel structures-remains a core challenge in cognitive science and machine learning. Although transformer-based large language models can exhibit strong performance on certain compositional tasks, the underlying mechanisms driving these abilities remain opaque, calling into question their interpretability. In this work, we identify and mechanistically interpret the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer. Using causal ablations, we validate the circuit and formalize its operation using a program-like description. We further demonstrate that this mechanistic understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably. Our findings advance the understanding of complex behaviors in transformers and highlight such insights can provide a direct pathway for model control.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small handle binary truth values in syllogistic prompts, and what circuits are responsible for logical reasoning in these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies circuits in GPT-2 small that handle syllogistic reasoning, uncovering binary mechanisms such as negation via negative attention heads and modulation via MLPs, and shows these circuits achieve high faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: By relating the findings on syllogistic reasoning circuits to prior IOI analysis, the paper provides new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs, contributing to a broader understanding of model reasoning and future mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Identified three distinct circuits for simple, opposite, and complex syllogisms in GPT-2 small.
Discovered a binary negation mechanism where negative truth heads produce the opposite token, aided by MLPs that rescale the residual stream.
Found empirical evidence for binary opposite tasks, showing the same attention heads flip their influence on logit difference between simple and opposite syllogisms.
Advanced interpretability of model components, detailing the roles of truth heads, negative truth heads, truth modulation heads, induction heads, and duplicate statement identifier heads.
Demonstrated that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance on the simple syllogism task.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous mechanistic interpretability research has primarily focused on linguistic tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, such as "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is'', which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that explain GPT-2 small’s logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token that does not appear in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model’s performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs. We believe these insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and benefit future research in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Moving Beyond Next-Token Prediction: Transformers are Context-Sensitive Language Generators
papers.research_question: How can Transformers be understood as stochastic approximations of left context-sensitive languages, bridging formal language theory and their generative power?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reframes Transformers as stochastic approximations of left context-sensitive languages, providing a formal language theory perspective that explains their human-like generative power.
papers.conclusion: Transformers stochastically approximate context-sensitive languages, bridging the gap between formal language theory and their practical generative power, and laying a foundation for future generative AI theory and applications.
papers.key_findings:
Next-token prediction in Transformers can be interpreted as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left context-sensitive language (CSL) production rules.
Autoregressive generation in Transformers can be reinterpreted through the lens of formal language theory, specifically as derivations of left CSLs.
Transformers function as stochastic approximations of context-sensitive languages, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence.
future_direction: Exploring expansions to general forms of context-sensitive grammars within autoregressive generation for improvements in performance and computational resource utilization.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Transformers, have demonstrated human-like intelligence capabilities, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper presents a novel framework for interpreting LLMs as probabilistic left context-sensitive languages (CSLs) generators. We hypothesize that Transformers can be effectively decomposed into three fundamental components: context windows, attention mechanisms, and autoregressive generation frameworks. This decomposition allows for the development of more flexible and interpretable computational models, moving beyond the traditional view of attention and autoregression as inseparable processes. We argue that next-token predictions can be understood as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left CSL production rules, providing an intuitive explanation for how simple token predictions can yield human-like intelligence outputs. Given that all CSLs are left context-sensitive (Penttonen, 1974), we conclude that Transformers stochastically approximate CSLs, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence. This interpretation bridges the gap between Formal Language Theory and the observed generative power of Transformers, laying a foundation for future advancements in generative AI theory and applications. Our novel perspective on Transformer architectures will foster a deeper understanding of LLMs and their future potentials.

papers.title: What do language models model? Transformers, automata, and the format of thought
papers.research_question: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we’ve trained them on?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers model the corpus rather than human linguistic capacities, due to the linear format of the residual stream, and they do so by emulating shortcut automata as suggested by Liu et al. (2022).
papers.conclusion: Language models are not modeling human thought but have learned to use language as a technology in a different way, by emulating automata that generate the corpus via shortcut solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit permutation invariance (unmasked) or substring invariance (masked), which implies the residual stream has at most a linear format.
Human cognitive science indicates that linguistic capabilities require supralinear formats for computation.
Therefore, transformers do not process language in the way humans do and do not model human linguistic capacities.
Transformers can be understood as calculating the input-to-state function of an automaton that generates the corpus, using parallel 'shortcut' solutions.
The transformer architecture is powerful because it eschews structured representations in favor of learning transformations that capture the structure of the domain.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on very simple LLMs: encoder-only transformers performing next-token autoregressive tasks.
The paper is a draft in progress and the author is not entirely happy with it, though the general argument is stood by.
papers.abstract: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we've trained them on? I give a non-deflationary defence of the latter position. Cognitive science tells us that linguistic capabilities in humans rely supralinear formats for computation. The transformer architecture, by contrast, supports at best a linear formats for processing. This argument will rely primarily on certain invariants of the computational architecture of transformers. I then suggest a positive story about what transformers are doing, focusing on Liu et al. (2022)'s intriguing speculations about shortcut automata. I conclude with why I don't think this is a terribly deflationary story. Language is not (just) a means for expressing inner state but also a kind of 'discourse machine' that lets us make new language given appropriate context. We have learned to use this technology in one way; LLMs have also learned to use it too, but via very different means.

papers.title: The Process of Categorical Clipping at the Core of the Genesis of Concepts in Synthetic Neural Cognition
papers.research_question: How does the process of categorical outlining (clipping) manifest in terms of cognitive and categorical properties within neural networks, specifically how does the aggregation function separate a form from a background?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the process of categorical clipping in neural networks, showing how neurons create new functional categories by selectively extracting subdimensions from precursor categories through a process of reflective abstraction, involving categorical reduction, selectivity, and segmentation of embedding dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Categorical outlining in synthetic cognition is a process of reflective abstraction that constructs new categories by recombining selected embedding dimensions from precursor categories, rather than merely extracting pre-existing forms.
papers.key_findings:
Categorical outlining involves the selective extraction of specific embedding dimensions from the initial embedding space, rather than random selection.
The extracted subdimensions are categorically convergent and homogeneous, indicating a non-random process.
The process is consistent with Piaget's stages of reflective abstraction, involving abstraction, reflection, and reasoning.
Categorical outlining constructs new categories by recombining selected embedding dimensions, rather than simply separating pre-existing forms.
The process demonstrates categorical selectivity, with a minority of tokens becoming 'taken' and associated with specific embedding dimensions.
papers.abstract: This article investigates, within the field of neuropsychology of artificial intelligence, the process of categorical segmentation performed by language models. This process involves, across different neural layers, the creation of new functional categorical dimensions to analyze the input textual data and perform the required tasks. Each neuron in a multilayer perceptron (MLP) network is associated with a specific category, generated by three factors carried by the neural aggregation function: categorical priming, categorical attention, and categorical phasing. At each new layer, these factors govern the formation of new categories derived from the categories of precursor neurons. Through a process of categorical clipping, these new categories are created by selectively extracting specific subdimensions from the preceding categories, constructing a distinction between a form and a categorical background. We explore several cognitive characteristics of this synthetic clipping in an exploratory manner: categorical reduction, categorical selectivity, separation of initial embedding dimensions, and segmentation of categorical zones.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
