papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully embeds interpretability into the model's architecture through discrete symbols and gating, providing a step towards trustworthy AI by making the decision process transparent and traceable.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model achieves competitive classification accuracy on the AG News dataset while providing verifiable reasoning traces.
The gated fine-tuning strategy effectively enhances the purity of learned symbols and the sparsity of decisions.
The model's internal decision process, including intuition symbols and gating confidence, is transparent and traceable, enabling detailed analysis.
The two-phase, two-step training framework (Iterative Refinement Training) successfully cultivates a model with specialized intuitive capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are primarily conducted on a news classification dataset (AG News), which is relatively domain-specific, limiting the verification of generalizability to more diverse and complex NLP tasks.
Hyperparameters such as purity_lambda and gated_focus_lambda were set manually, which might limit the model's optimal performance.
future_direction: Model scaling by increasing d_model or codebook_size for more complex tasks.
Architectural evolution by introducing a Hierarchical Quantized VAE (HQ-VAE) for hierarchical semantic understanding.
Applying the architecture to other, more complex NLP tasks such as sequence labeling or text summarization.
Exploring automated hyperparameter tuning methods for weights like λpurity and λfocus.
Developing more advanced visualization tools, such as dynamically generating semantic descriptions for symbols.
papers.abstract: We present a framework where neural models develop an AI Mother Tongue, a native symbolic language that simultaneously supports intuitive reasoning, compositional symbol chains, and inherent interpretability. Unlike post-hoc explanation methods, our approach embeds reasoning directly into the model's representations: symbols capture meaningful semantic patterns, chains trace decision paths, and gated induction mechanisms guide selective focus, yielding transparent yet flexible reasoning. We introduce complementary training objectives to enhance symbol purity and decision sparsity, and employ a sequential specialization strategy to first build broad symbolic competence and then refine intuitive judgments. Experiments on AI tasks demonstrate competitive accuracy alongside verifiable reasoning traces, showing that AI Mother Tongue can serve as a unified mechanism for interpretability, intuition, and symbolic reasoning in neural models.

papers.title: A Theory of Emergent In-Context Learning as Implicit Structure Induction
papers.research_question: When and how does in-context learning (ICL) emerge from generic next-token prediction in language models? The paper investigates the conditions under which ICL capabilities arise from the recombination of compositional operations found in natural language pretraining data.
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical framework showing that in-context learning emerges from next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient compositional structure, and validates this with experiments showing ICL emergence in scaled transformer LMs.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in language models arises from the recombination of compositional structure found in linguistic data, and the paper provides a theoretical and empirical step towards understanding this emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when scaling model parameters and data on compositionally structured pretraining distributions.
Prompting models to output intermediate steps (chain-of-thought) provides a theoretical and empirical benefit over direct prompting.
The success of ICL depends on the complexity of the task's compositional description and the iteration complexity of the pretraining data structure.
Probing experiments indicate that in-context learning is supported by the model learning a representation of the input's compositional structure.
The theoretical bounds are independent of the size of the object universe |Ω|, and empirical performance can even improve with larger |Ω|.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis considers an idealized predictor with infinite data and capacity, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world finite transformer models.
future_direction: Exploring more complex compositional structures and their learnability.
Investigating the application of the theory to real-world natural language data and models.
Extending the analysis to longer chains of reasoning and more complex task compositions.
papers.abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) leads to an emergent capacity to learn in-context from example demonstrations. Despite progress, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. We argue that in-context learning relies on recombination of compositional operations found in natural language data. We derive an information-theoretic bound showing how in-context learning abilities arise from generic next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient amounts of compositional structure, under linguistically motivated assumptions. A second bound provides a theoretical justification for the empirical success of prompting LLMs to output intermediate steps towards an answer. To validate theoretical predictions, we introduce a controlled setup for inducing in-context learning; unlike previous approaches, it accounts for the compositional nature of language. Trained transformers can perform in-context learning for a range of tasks, in a manner consistent with the theoretical results. Mirroring real-world LLMs in a miniature setup, in-context learning emerges when scaling parameters and data, and models perform better when prompted to output intermediate steps. Probing shows that in-context learning is supported by a representation of the input's compositional structure. Taken together, these results provide a step towards theoretical understanding of emergent behavior in large language models.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Abstraction via exemplars? A representational case study on lexical category inference in BERT
papers.research_question: How does lexical category abstraction emerge in BERT through the compressed encoding of training exemplars?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in BERT, lexical category abstraction emerges through the compressed encoding of exemplars, as evidenced by representational changes aligning with known category regions.
papers.conclusion: The study supports the abstraction-via-exemplars account, showing that linguistic abstraction in BERT arises from compressed exemplar encoding.
papers.key_findings:
After training on fill-in-the-blank inputs, BERT's embeddings for novel tokens move closer in representation space to known exemplars of their lexical category.
Novel tokens initialized with values from category-exemplar regions in 2D space achieve above-chance accuracy on lexical category inference without additional training.
This provides evidence that abstraction-like behavior in language models can arise from the encoding of training exemplars rather than explicit abstractions.
papers.abstract: Exemplar based accounts are often considered to be in direct opposition to pure linguistic abstraction in explaining language learners' ability to generalize to novel expressions. However, the recent success of neural network language models on linguistically sensitive tasks suggests that perhaps abstractions can arise via the encoding of exemplars. We provide empirical evidence for this claim by adapting an existing experiment that studies how an LM (BERT) generalizes the usage of novel tokens that belong to lexical categories such as Noun/Verb/Adjective/Adverb from exposure to only a single instance of their usage. We analyze the representational behavior of the novel tokens in these experiments, and find that BERT's capacity to generalize to unseen expressions involving the use of these novel tokens constitutes the movement of novel token representations towards regions of known category exemplars in two-dimensional space. Our results suggest that learners' encoding of exemplars can indeed give rise to abstraction like behavior.

papers.title: Linguistics and Human Brain: A Perspective of Computational Neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can computational neuroscience bridge the methodological gap between linguistics and neuroscience to elucidate the language-brain relationship?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes interdisciplinary progress from a computational neuroscience perspective, outlining how it formalizes linguistic theories into testable models and uses large language models to advance model-brain alignment for understanding language processing.
papers.conclusion: This work aims to advance a comprehensive, mechanistic understanding of the language-brain relationship and promote computational neuroscience as a generative theoretical framework for testable neuro-computational accounts of language.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal interactions between language and perceptual systems (e.g., vision, music) exist and are partially captured by multimodal large models, providing tools for studying semantic coding.
Inter-brain neural coupling during communication shows alignment between speaker and listener neural systems, with coupling strength increasing with shared semantic representations.
Hierarchical computation in large language models aligns with brain processing, but differences exist, prompting debate on whether models implement genuine hierarchical computation or statistical learning.
Large language models and humans show similar sensitivities in learning strategies, such as in-context learning, revealing parallels in adaptive language processing.
Language plasticity in the brain, including acquisition and adaptation, can be studied through model-brain alignment, offering insights into neural mechanisms of learning and recovery.
papers.limitation:
Functional alignment without structural homology
Constraints on real-time validation
Biased research coverage
Narrow evaluation metrics
future_direction: Improving biological plausibility via spiking neural network–based language models
Developing cognitive-level alignment frameworks integrating memory, causality, and metacognition
Extending clinical applications and brain–computer interface applications
papers.abstract: Elucidating the language-brain relationship requires bridging the methodological gap between the abstract theoretical frameworks of linguistics and the empirical neural data of neuroscience. Serving as an interdisciplinary cornerstone, computational neuroscience formalizes the hierarchical and dynamic structures of language into testable neural models through modeling, simulation, and data analysis. This enables a computational dialogue between linguistic hypotheses and neural mechanisms. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly large language models (LLMs), have powerfully advanced this pursuit. Their high-dimensional representational spaces provide a novel scale for exploring the neural basis of linguistic processing, while the "model-brain alignment" framework offers a methodology to evaluate the biological plausibility of language-related theories.

papers.title: Deeper Insights Without Updates: The Power of In-Context Learning Over Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning capture implicit patterns better than fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns in tasks, and the authors propose circuit shift theory to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning significantly outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns within specific tasks and exhibits greater adaptability in problem-solving approaches, as evidenced by notable shifts in model circuits.
papers.key_findings:
ICL achieves higher accuracy than fine-tuning on implicit pattern detection tasks across models and tasks.
ICL is more robust to misleading data and out-of-distribution data compared to fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning plateaus quickly with more data, showing diminishing returns for implicit pattern detection.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods do not show significant improvement over full-parameter fine-tuning for implicit pattern detection.
ICL induces larger circuit shifts than fine-tuning, indicating a more significant change in the model's problem-solving approach.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is constrained by the specific nature of the implicit pattern detection tasks, limited to certain domains.
Circuit Shift analysis relies on activation patching and sensitivity analysis, which require further refinement and validation across different models and tasks.
Computational resources required for fine-tuning, especially with large models, may limit the feasibility of such experiments in broader settings.
A detailed cost-benefit analysis comparing ICL and fine-tuning in terms of computational efficiency and performance is needed.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) are two prevalent methods in imbuing large language models with task-specific knowledge. It is commonly believed that fine-tuning can surpass ICL given sufficient training samples as it allows the model to adjust its internal parameters based on the data. However, this paper presents a counterintuitive finding: For tasks with implicit patterns, ICL captures these patterns significantly better than fine-tuning. We developed several datasets featuring implicit patterns, such as sequences determining answers through parity or identifying reducible terms in calculations. We then evaluated the models' understanding of these patterns under both fine-tuning and ICL across models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The results indicate that models employing ICL can quickly grasp deep patterns and significantly improve accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning, despite utilizing thousands of times more training samples than ICL, achieved only limited improvements. We also proposed circuit shift theory from a mechanistic interpretability's view to explain why ICL wins.

papers.title: The Mechanics of Conceptual Interpretation in GPT Models: Interpretative Insights
papers.research_question: What are the observable representation patterns that characterise conceptual interpretation within language models? Can we localise specialised representational patterns to derive an interpretation model within language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces concept editing, a variation of knowledge editing, to uncover conceptualization mechanisms in LLMs, and through analysis of MLP, MHA, and hidden states, reveals distinct patterns of semantic processing.
papers.conclusion: The work elucidates how transformer models process semantic information through distinct component interactions, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
MLP layers employ key-value retrieval and context-dependent processing, focusing on specific lexical and semantic features.
MHA layers show distributed nature with higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration.
Hidden states emphasize the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process, indicating gradual information building.
Concept interpretation involves a collaborative process among model components, with compositionality being critical.
Patterns are consistent across languages (English and Spanish) and across alternative definitions, indicating robust processing strategies.
papers.abstract: Locating and editing knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their accuracy, safety, and inference rationale. We introduce ``concept editing'', an innovative variation of knowledge editing that uncovers conceptualisation mechanisms within these models. Using the reverse dictionary task, inference tracing, and input abstraction, we analyse the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Multi-Head Attention (MHA), and hidden state components of transformer models. Our results reveal distinct patterns: MLP layers employ key-value retrieval mechanism and context-dependent processing, which are highly associated with relative input tokens. MHA layers demonstrate a distributed nature with significant higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration. Hidden states emphasise the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process. We observe evidence of gradual information building and distributed representation. These observations elucidate how transformer models process semantic information, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques. Our work highlights the complex, layered nature of semantic processing in LLMs and the challenges of isolating and modifying specific concepts within these models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Lost in Translation: The Algorithmic Gap Between LMs and the Brain
papers.research_question: What is the algorithmic gap between language models and the human brain, and how can we bridge it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that despite computational-level equivalence in some tasks, language models diverge from human cognition at the algorithmic level, and proposes neuroscience-inspired architectural and training changes to bridge this gap.
papers.conclusion: The intelligence emerging from current LMs is fundamentally different from human cognition, and incorporating brain-inspired constraints may lead to AI with human-like flexibility and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language models and the brain show representational similarities but likely use different algorithms.
Current LMs lack brain-like features such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning.
Incorporating brain-inspired features could lead to more human-like AI and better models of cognition.
future_direction: Incorporate sparse connectivity and modularity (e.g., MoE, RIMs) in LMs.
Add internal states and recurrence to transformers.
Develop continual and curriculum learning methods for LMs.
Ground LMs in embodied and social interactions.
Integrate oscillatory dynamics and scaling laws with efficiency constraints.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) have achieved impressive performance on various linguistic tasks, but their relationship to human language processing in the brain remains unclear. This paper examines the gaps and overlaps between LMs and the brain at different levels of analysis, emphasizing the importance of looking beyond input-output behavior to examine and compare the internal processes of these systems. We discuss how insights from neuroscience, such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning, can inform the development of more biologically plausible language models. Furthermore, we explore the role of scaling laws in bridging the gap between LMs and human cognition, highlighting the need for efficiency constraints analogous to those in biological systems. By developing LMs that more closely mimic brain function, we aim to advance both artificial intelligence and our understanding of human cognition.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Why does in-context learning (ICL) emerge and then disappear (transience) during training, and what are the dynamics between ICL and other learning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The transience of in-context learning (ICL) is explained by coopetition (cooperative and competitive dynamics) between ICL and a newly identified strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), where shared sub-circuits enable ICL emergence before CIWL asymptotically dominates.
papers.conclusion: Strategy coopetition between ICL and CIWL explains the emergence and transience of ICL, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of how capabilities dynamically trade off during transformer training.
papers.key_findings:
The asymptotic strategy after ICL transience is a hybrid called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), which depends on both in-weights information and the presence of the correct label in context.
ICL and CIWL share critical sub-circuits (e.g., Layer 2 induction heads), leading to cooperative dynamics that enable ICL emergence.
ICL emergence is only possible when CIWL is not fully formed, and ICL is faster to emerge but asymptotically dominated by CIWL.
A minimal mathematical model captures the coopetition dynamics and explains transience.
Matching context and query exemplars in the data can make ICL persistent by removing the asymptotic bias towards CIWL.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that, after the disappearance of ICL, the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term "context-constrained in-weights learning" (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term "strategy coopetition." We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

papers.title: Three tiers of computation in transformers and in brain architectures
papers.research_question: What enabled transformer-based A.I. models to suddenly generate fluent natural language where previous AI models had failed, and why are current transformer-based models having difficulty obtaining arithmetic and logic skills?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark based on the grammar-automata hierarchy to evaluate computational capabilities, and provides a framework linking transitions in computational tiers to language and logic abilities in transformers and humans.
papers.conclusion: The grammar-automata hierarchy provides a principled framework for understanding the capabilities and limitations of transformers and humans, suggesting that architectural augmentations (like multiple memory stacks) are needed for logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs (under tens of billions of parameters) do not reliably process any of the formal grammar inputs.
Mid-sized LMs show some recognition of context-free grammar (CFG) but are unreliable on higher-level grammars.
Large LLMs and humans robustly recognize CFG and indexed grammar (IXG) strings, but not context-sensitive grammar (CSG) strings.
Interpolated Augmented LLMs (IALLMs) recognize CFG and IXG and also a significant portion (up to 44%) of CSG sentences.
The transition from single-stack to multi-stack memory in the automata hierarchy corresponds to the transition from language to logic abilities.
future_direction: Explore architectural changes to provide separate external memory stores to expand transformers to higher computational tiers.
Investigate the broader space of specific hybrid architectures, including interpolations of neurosymbolic methods.
papers.abstract: Human language and logic abilities are computationally quantified within the well-studied grammar-automata hierarchy. We identify three hierarchical tiers and two corresponding transitions and show their correspondence to specific abilities in transformer-based language models (LMs). These emergent abilities have often been described in terms of scaling; we show that it is the transition between tiers, rather than scaled size itself, that determines a system's capabilities. Specifically, humans effortlessly process language yet require critical training to perform arithmetic or logical reasoning tasks; and LMs possess language abilities absent from predecessor systems, yet still struggle with logical processing. We submit a novel benchmark of computational power, provide empirical evaluations of humans and fifteen LMs, and, most significantly, provide a theoretically grounded framework to promote careful thinking about these crucial topics. The resulting principled analyses provide explanatory accounts of the abilities and shortfalls of LMs, and suggest actionable insights into the expansion of their logic abilities.

papers.title: Relational reasoning and inductive bias in transformers and large language models
papers.research_question: How do transformers perform transitive inference, and how do inductive biases differ between in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL) strategies?
papers.core_contribution: IWL naturally induces transitive inference with symbolic distance and terminal item effects, while ICL models develop induction circuits that fail to generalize; however, pre-training on linear regression enables transitive inference in ICL without induction circuits.
papers.conclusion: Both the training regime and the geometric structure of induced representations critically determine transformers' capacity for transitive inference.
papers.key_findings:
IWL models exhibit transitive inference and show symbolic distance and terminal item effects despite training only on adjacent pairs.
ICL models trained only on adjacent pairs fail to generalize and rely on induction circuits implementing match-and-copy strategies.
Pre-training transformers on in-context linear regression tasks enables transitive inference in ICL without forming induction circuits.
Linear geometric prompts improve transitive inference in large language models, while circular prompts impair performance, especially when models cannot rely on stored knowledge.
The advantage of linear over circular prompting increases with model size for incongruent item pairs.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analyses (PCA, ablation studies, attention patterns) were restricted to small transformer architectures for interpretability; internal mechanisms in LLMs remain opaque.
The transitive inference task is a simple example of relational reasoning which might not capture all real-world scenarios.
Results are empirical rather than theoretical.
future_direction: Combine experiments with advanced mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLMs.
Use transitive inference as a benchmark for evaluating model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have demonstrated remarkable reasoning abilities, but the mechanisms underlying relational reasoning remain poorly understood. We investigate how transformers perform \textit{transitive inference}, a classic relational reasoning task which requires inference indirectly related items (e.g., if $A>B$ and $B>C$, then $A>C$), comparing in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL) strategies. We find that IWL naturally induces a generalization bias towards transitive inference despite training only on adjacent items, whereas ICL models develop induction circuits implementing match-and-copy strategies that fail to encode hierarchical relationships. However, when pre-trained on in-context linear regression tasks, transformers successfully exhibit in-context generalizable transitive inference, displaying both \textit{symbolic distance} and \textit{terminal item effects} characteristic of human and animal performance, without forming induction circuits. We extend these findings to large language models, demonstrating that prompting with linear geometric scaffolds improves transitive inference, while circular geometries (which violate transitivity by allowing wraparound) impair performance, particularly when models cannot rely on stored knowledge. Together, these results reveal that both the training regime and the geometric structure of induced representations critically determine transformers' capacity for transitive inference.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
papers.research_question: What is the function of feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models? The paper shows they operate as key-value memories.
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformer language models function as key-value memories, where keys capture input patterns and values represent output distributions, and the model's final output is constructed by composing and refining these memories across layers.
papers.conclusion: Feed-forward layers in transformers act as pattern-detecting key-value memories, and the model's output is gradually constructed by composing these memories within layers and refining them across layers via residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Keys in feed-forward layers correlate with human-interpretable input patterns, with lower layers capturing shallow patterns (e.g., n-grams) and upper layers capturing semantic patterns.
Values in upper layers induce distributions over the output vocabulary that correlate with the next-token distribution of the patterns in the corresponding keys.
The output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of hundreds of active memories, rarely dominated by a single memory cell.
Residual connections act as a refinement mechanism, with the feed-forward layer often vetoing the residual's top prediction to shift probability mass to other candidates.
The model's final prediction is often determined in the lower layers, with upper layers refining the confidence and occasionally changing the prediction.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to one language model and dataset, and the assumption that all layers operate in the same embedding space may not hold for lower layers.
future_direction: Investigating the transformation of embedding spaces across layers and the interplay between feed-forward and self-attention layers.
Extending the analysis to other transformer models, such as BERT encoders and neural translation models.
Exploring practical implications for interpretability methods, data privacy (e.g., membership inference), and architectural innovations.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward layers constitute two-thirds of a transformer model's parameters, yet their role in the network remains under-explored. We show that feed-forward layers in transformerbased language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary. Our experiments show that the learned patterns are human-interpretable, and that lower layers tend to capture shallow patterns, while upper layers learn more semantic ones. The values complement the keys' input patterns by inducing output distributions that concentrate probability mass on tokens likely to appear immediately after each pattern, particularly in the upper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that the output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of its memories, which is subsequently refined throughout the model's layers via residual connections to produce the final output distribution.

papers.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is in-context learning (ICL) in transformers a persistent phenomenon, or does it emerge and then disappear (become transient) during training?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning (ICL) in transformers is often transient: it emerges and then disappears during training, even as training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for in-weights learning (IWL).
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is often transient, emphasizing the importance of validation metrics, early stopping, or regularization to preserve ICL capabilities during training.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges and then disappears (is transient) during training, while IWL accuracy increases.
ICL transience occurs across a range of model sizes (depth, embedding dimension), dataset sizes (number of classes, exemplars per class), and dataset types (Omniglot images, LLaMa token embeddings).
Data distributional properties, such as a larger number of classes or a Zipfian skew, can postpone the transience of ICL.
L2 regularization can mitigate or eliminate ICL transience, potentially by favoring the lower-norm ICL circuit.
Preliminary evidence suggests ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits for resources in the transformer's residual stream.
future_direction: Explore the effect of alternate optimizers or initialization schemes on the transience of ICL.
Connect findings to natural language settings and large-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to "overtrain" transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

papers.title: Unifying Attention Heads and Task Vectors via Hidden State Geometry in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and task vectors jointly shape the hidden state geometry in in-context learning, and can they be unified in a single framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a unified framework linking attention heads and task vectors through the geometry of hidden states in in-context learning, revealing a two-stage mechanism where separability emerges early and alignment develops later.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of the underlying mechanisms of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
ICL improves classification primarily by enhancing the alignment of query hidden states with label unembedding vectors, not by increasing separability.
ICL proceeds as a two-stage process: early layers increase hidden-state separability, while middle-to-late layers improve alignment.
Previous Token Heads (PTHs) drive the early increase in separability.
Induction Heads (IHs) enhance alignment in later layers by amplifying hidden state components along the unembedding directions.
The two-stage phase transition pattern is robust across different ICL settings, models, and extends to generation tasks.
papers.abstract: The unusual properties of in-context learning (ICL) have prompted investigations into the internal mechanisms of large language models. Prior work typically focuses on either special attention heads or task vectors at specific layers, but lacks a unified framework linking these components to the evolution of hidden states across layers that ultimately produce the model's output. In this paper, we propose such a framework for ICL in classification tasks by analyzing two geometric factors that govern performance: the separability and alignment of query hidden states. A fine-grained analysis of layer-wise dynamics reveals a striking two-stage mechanism: separability emerges in early layers, while alignment develops in later layers. Ablation studies further show that Previous Token Heads drive separability, while Induction Heads and task vectors enhance alignment. Our findings thus bridge the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of ICL's underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Beyond Induction Heads: In-Context Meta Learning Induces Multi-Phase Circuit Emergence
papers.research_question: How is meta-learning ability in in-context learning acquired during training, specifically through the dynamics of the model's internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-learning ability in in-context learning is acquired through multiple phases, each with a distinct circuit emerging, contrasting with the single-phase change observed in induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Multi-phase circuit emergence underlies the acquisition of meta-learning capabilities in in-context learning, and these findings help bridge the gap between controlled mechanistic interpretability experiments and practical large language model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model undergoes three learning phases (Non-Context, Semi-Context, Full-Context) with distinct circuits emerging in each phase.
Sudden jumps in accuracy align with the abrupt emergence of these circuits.
The Semi-Context Circuit explains the random-label robustness phenomenon observed in large language models.
In multi-head settings, circuits emerge in parallel, leading to smoother accuracy improvements while hidden circuit changes still occur.
Similar circuit patterns (chunk example in early layers, label attention in later layers) are observed in pretrained models like GPT2-XL on real-world tasks.
papers.limitation: The work uses a simplified transformer model and synthetic data, which may not fully capture the complexity of real large language model behaviors.
future_direction: Connecting controlled experiments in mechanistic interpretability to realistic use-cases of large language models.
Bridging geometric perspectives (like Local Learning Coefficient) with mechanistic circuit analyses to enrich interpretability methodologies.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit In-Context Learning (ICL), where predictions are made adaptively based on context. While prior work links induction heads to ICL through a sudden jump in accuracy, this can only account for ICL when the answer is included within the context. However, an important property of practical ICL in large language models is the ability to meta-learn how to solve tasks from context, rather than just copying answers from context; how such an ability is obtained during training is largely unexplored. In this paper, we experimentally clarify how such meta-learning ability is acquired by analyzing the dynamics of the model's circuit during training. Specifically, we extend the copy task from previous research into an In-Context Meta Learning setting, where models must infer a task from examples to answer queries. Interestingly, in this setting, we find that there are multiple phases in the process of acquiring such abilities, and that a unique circuit emerges in each phase, contrasting with the single-phases change in induction heads. The emergence of such circuits can be related to several phenomena known in large language models, and our analysis lead to a deeper understanding of the source of the transformer's ICL ability.

papers.title: Systematic Generalization and Emergent Structures in Transformers Trained on Structured Tasks
papers.research_question: How and when can transformers acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer causal transformers with label-based order encoding can learn algorithmic tasks and generalize to longer sequences, exhibiting signs of task decomposition and shared computation across tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve structured algorithmic tasks and generalize systematically, with attention layers developing task decomposition and shared computation.
papers.key_findings:
Label-based order encoding enables strong length generalization in transformers on algorithmic tasks.
Two-layer transformers are sufficient to solve multi-level sorting tasks, while single-layer models fail.
Attention patterns in two-layer models show task decomposition: first layer attends to items in the same feature group, second layer attends to the next output token.
In multi-task learning, transformers can learn multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize to longer sequences, with attention heads showing shared computation across tasks.
Task-conditioned item representations are reorganized according to the task structure, showing clustering by relevant features.
papers.limitation:
Label-based encoding alone would not represent true item distance information.
The tasks are simple and synthetic, and may not capture the complexity of natural data.
future_direction: Explore learning and generalization dynamics in transformer-based agents to understand the acquisition of task-conditioned, multi-level behavioral policies in structured environments.
Characterize the degree of possible computational modularity in multi-headed attention in relation to task structures.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have seen great success in natural language processing and machine vision, where task objectives such as next word prediction and image classification benefit from nuanced context sensitivity across high-dimensional inputs. However, there is an ongoing debate about how and when transformers can acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization. Here, we explore how well a causal transformer can perform a set of algorithmic tasks, including copying, sorting, and hierarchical compositions of these operations. We demonstrate strong generalization to sequences longer than those used in training by replacing the standard positional encoding typically used in transformers with labels arbitrarily paired with items in the sequence. We search for the layer and head configuration sufficient to solve these tasks, then probe for signs of systematic processing in latent representations and attention patterns. We show that two-layer transformers learn reliable solutions to multi-level problems, develop signs of task decomposition, and encode input items in a way that encourages the exploitation of shared computation across related tasks. These results provide key insights into how attention layers support structured computation both within a task and across multiple tasks.

papers.title: A Philosophical Introduction to Language Models - Part II: The Way Forward
papers.research_question: What are the philosophical implications of recent progress in LLMs, particularly regarding interpretability, multimodality, consciousness, reproducibility, and their relevance to modeling human cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a philosophical exploration of issues raised by LLMs, arguing for the importance of mechanistic interpretability through causal intervention methods and discussing the implications of multimodal extensions, consciousness debates, and reproducibility concerns.
papers.conclusion: LLM-like systems may be relevant to modeling aspects of human cognition if their architectural characteristics and learning scenarios are adequately constrained, but further research is needed to address interpretability and reproducibility challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Benchmarks for LLMs are limited by saturation, gamification, contamination, and construct validity issues, which undermine their reliability for assessing model capacities.
Causal intervention methods, such as ablation and activation editing, are necessary for achieving mechanistic understanding of LLMs' internal representations and computations.
Multimodal models often exhibit compositional failures due to their training objectives (e.g., contrastive learning) rather than inherent architectural limitations of the Transformer.
There are ongoing debates about whether LLMs could meet minimal criteria for consciousness, though current evidence is insufficient and the analogy to biological consciousness is problematic.
LLM research faces significant issues of secrecy and reproducibility, which hinder scientific progress and trust in reported capabilities.
future_direction: Advancing mechanistic interpretability through causal intervention methods to understand LLMs' internal mechanisms.
Addressing reproducibility and secrecy issues in LLM research to foster open scientific inquiry.
Exploring the potential of LLMs as models of human cognition by constraining their architecture and learning scenarios appropriately.
papers.abstract: In this paper, the second of two companion pieces, we explore novel philosophical questions raised by recent progress in large language models (LLMs) that go beyond the classical debates covered in the first part. We focus particularly on issues related to interpretability, examining evidence from causal intervention methods about the nature of LLMs' internal representations and computations. We also discuss the implications of multimodal and modular extensions of LLMs, recent debates about whether such systems may meet minimal criteria for consciousness, and concerns about secrecy and reproducibility in LLM research. Finally, we discuss whether LLM-like systems may be relevant to modeling aspects of human cognition, if their architectural characteristics and learning scenario are adequately constrained.

papers.title: Algorithmic Phase Transitions in Language Models: A Mechanistic Case Study of Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How do language models achieve zero-shot performance on some tasks but not others? Specifically, do they use stable algorithms across related subtasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concepts of algorithmic stability and algorithmic phase transitions, and shows that language models exhibit sharp algorithmic phase transitions even on simple arithmetic tasks, which may explain poor generalization.
papers.conclusion: Language models are algorithmically unstable for two-operand addition, and this instability may be a barrier for generalization in logical reasoning. The introduced interpretability technique can help evaluate model design choices and serve as a diagnostic tool.
papers.key_findings:
Gemma-2-2b uses different computational subcircuits for addition problems with different digit lengths, indicating algorithmic instability.
The model undergoes sharp algorithmic phase transitions between symmetric, boundary, and interior addition tasks.
The structure of the identified subcircuits varies: symmetric tasks show top-heavy circuits, boundary tasks show two peaks of activation, and interior tasks show diffuse circuits.
Algorithmic instability correlates with lack of generalization in arithmetic performance.
The paper introduces methods to quantify algorithmic changes using activation patching and clustering techniques.
papers.limitation:
Relies on activation patching, which has known limitations.
Operationalizes algorithmic changes as structural changes, which may not capture all aspects of algorithmic change.
future_direction: Test the robustness of identified subcircuits by perturbing the weights of the network.
Explore other methods to quantify algorithmic changes beyond structural similarity.
papers.abstract: Zero-shot capabilities of large language models make them powerful tools for solving a range of tasks without explicit training. It remains unclear, however, how these models achieve such performance, or why they can zero-shot some tasks but not others. In this paper, we shed some light on this phenomenon by defining and investigating algorithmic stability in language models -- changes in problem-solving strategy employed by the model as a result of changes in task specification. We focus on a task where algorithmic stability is needed for generalization: two-operand arithmetic. Surprisingly, we find that Gemma-2-2b employs substantially different computational models on closely related subtasks, i.e. four-digit versus eight-digit addition. Our findings suggest that algorithmic instability may be a contributing factor to language models' poor zero-shot performance across certain logical reasoning tasks, as they struggle to abstract different problem-solving strategies and smoothly transition between them.

papers.title: Abstraction Induces the Brain Alignment of Language and Speech Models
papers.research_question: Why do intermediate hidden states of language and speech models predict brain responses? Is this due to shared meaning abstraction rather than next-word prediction properties?
papers.core_contribution: The correspondence between speech/language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction, not next-word prediction. The intrinsic dimension of representations peaks in intermediate layers and strongly predicts brain encoding performance.
papers.conclusion: Meaning abstraction, as captured by high intrinsic dimension, is the key driver of model-brain similarity, and prediction objectives alone are insufficient for achieving this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Layerwise surprisal does not account for layerwise encoding performance, ruling out next-token predictivity as the primary driver.
Intrinsic dimension (Id) peaks in intermediate layers and tracks the construction of higher-order linguistic features (semantic abstraction).
Layerwise Id strongly correlates with layerwise brain encoding performance across models and imaging modalities.
Id and encoding performance grow in tandem over model pre-training, indicating the relationship emerges from learning.
Finetuning models to better predict brain activity causally increases both the Id and semantic content of their representations.
papers.limitation:
High intrinsic dimension is necessary but not sufficient for high neural predictivity, as demonstrated by random Fourier features.
The relationship between Id and encoding performance is weaker for some speech models (e.g., WavLM-base-plus) where low-level acoustic similarity may dominate.
future_direction: Developing better methods for extracting task-relevant structure from naturalistic data to advance encoding models.
Further investigation of linear dimensionality measures in relation to abstraction and encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models and speech audio models predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most effective for this unique and highly general transfer task? We give evidence that the correspondence between speech and language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction and not their next-word prediction properties. In particular, models construct higher-order linguistic features in their middle layers, cued by a peak in the layerwise intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity. We show that a layer's intrinsic dimension strongly predicts how well it explains fMRI and ECoG signals; that the relation between intrinsic dimension and brain predictivity arises over model pre-training; and finetuning models to better predict the brain causally increases both representations' intrinsic dimension and their semantic content. Results suggest that semantic richness, high intrinsic dimension, and brain predictivity mirror each other, and that the key driver of model-brain similarity is rich meaning abstraction of the inputs, where language modeling is a task sufficiently complex (but perhaps not the only) to require it.

papers.title: Are Transformers Able to Reason by Connecting Separated Knowledge in Training Data?
papers.research_question: When and how can transformers perform compositional reasoning by connecting fragmented knowledge, and what internal mechanisms enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can perform compositional reasoning on the FTCT task via few-shot chain-of-thought prompting, enabled by induction heads and attention assignment, with emergence depending on model complexity and training-testing similarity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can reason by connecting separated knowledge when provided with few-shot chain-of-thought prompts, and this ability is facilitated by induction heads and attention assignment mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting enables transformers to perform compositional reasoning by revealing correct vertices order.
Compositional reasoning emerges when the relative knowledge ratio (training child chain length to testing chain length) exceeds 0.3.
Multi-layer attention mechanisms (at least 2 layers and 2 heads) are necessary for compositional reasoning.
Transformers learn an underlying program during training, implemented via induction heads for in-context learning and attention assignment for parent retrieving.
The ability to reason compositionally is robust to noise in testing data but limited when intermediate steps are incomplete.
papers.limitation: Transformers trained on FTCT exhibit limited proficiency in reasoning with incomplete intermediate steps.
papers.abstract: Humans exhibit remarkable compositional reasoning by integrating knowledge from various sources. For example, if someone learns ( B = f(A) ) from one source and ( C = g(B) ) from another, they can deduce ( C=g(B)=g(f(A)) ) even without encountering ( ABC ) together, showcasing the generalization ability of human intelligence. In this paper, we introduce a synthetic learning task, "FTCT" (Fragmented at Training, Chained at Testing), to validate the potential of Transformers in replicating this skill and interpret its inner mechanism. In the training phase, data consist of separated knowledge fragments from an overall causal graph. During testing, Transformers must infer complete causal graph traces by integrating these fragments. Our findings demonstrate that few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting enables Transformers to perform compositional reasoning on FTCT by revealing correct combinations of fragments, even if such combinations were absent in the training data.
