papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that SAE feature similarity is a useful measure for cross-architectural universality, revealing significant similarity between Transformer and Mamba features and circuits, with an Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE features in Pythia and Mamba are similar, with high Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation (MPPC).
Feature similarity is affected by semantic complexity; simpler features have higher correlation.
Induction circuits in Mamba are analogous to those in Transformers, but with an Off-by-One motif where information is written into the SSM state at the next token.
SAE features show depth specialization across architectures, with matched features appearing at proportionally similar layers.
The neuron baseline shows almost zero similarity, indicating SAEs are better for cross-architecture comparison than neuron-based methods.
papers.limitation:
SAEs may not capture all true features and might capture combinations of features rather than the features themselves.
Circuit universality analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative automated comparison tools.
future_direction: Automating circuit discovery and comparison for quantitative measurement of circuit universality.
Further study on the Off-by-One motif in Mamba circuits to understand its purpose and formation.
papers.abstract: The hypothesis of Universality in interpretability suggests that different neural networks may converge to implement similar algorithms on similar tasks. In this work, we investigate two mainstream architectures for language modeling, namely Transformers and Mambas, to explore the extent of their mechanistic similarity. We propose to use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to isolate interpretable features from these models and show that most features are similar in these two models. We also validate the correlation between feature similarity and Universality. We then delve into the circuit-level analysis of Mamba models and find that the induction circuits in Mamba are structurally analogous to those in Transformers. We also identify a nuanced difference we call \emph{Off-by-One motif}: The information of one token is written into the SSM state in its next position. Whilst interaction between tokens in Transformers does not exhibit such trend.

papers.title: Encoding of phonology in a recurrent neural model of grounded speech
papers.research_question: How is phonological information encoded in the layers of a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech, and how does the encoding change across layers with respect to form and meaning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how phoneme representations are encoded across layers of a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech, finding that phonological information is strongest in lower layers but persists in higher layers, and that the attention mechanism attenuates phonology to achieve semantic invariance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that phonological information is encoded most strongly in lower layers of the model, but persists in higher layers, and that the attention mechanism filters out phonological details to focus on semantic meaning.
papers.key_findings:
Phoneme representations are most salient in the lower layers of the model, where low-level signals are processed at a fine-grained level.
A large amount of phonological information is retained at the top recurrent layer.
The attention mechanism following the top recurrent layer significantly attenuates encoding of phonology and makes utterance embeddings more invariant to synonymy.
Hierarchical clustering of phoneme representations learned by the network shows an organizational structure similar to linguistic classifications.
The model can discriminate phonemes with high accuracy, and lower layers are more informative for this task than higher layers or input features.
papers.limitation: The model is trained on synthetic speech, which is easier to process than natural human-generated speech.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to grounded human speech to investigate whether context and speaker-invariant phoneme representations can be learned from natural, noisy input.
Compare the results to similar analyses applied to neuroimaging data.
papers.abstract: We study the representation and encoding of phonemes in a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech. We use a model which processes images and their spoken descriptions, and projects the visual and auditory representations into the same semantic space. We perform a number of analyses on how information about individual phonemes is encoded in the MFCC features extracted from the speech signal, and the activations of the layers of the model. Via experiments with phoneme decoding and phoneme discrimination we show that phoneme representations are most salient in the lower layers of the model, where low-level signals are processed at a fine-grained level, although a large amount of phonological information is retain at the top recurrent layer. We further find out that the attention mechanism following the top recurrent layer significantly attenuates encoding of phonology and makes the utterance embeddings much more invariant to synonymy. Moreover, a hierarchical clustering of phoneme representations learned by the network shows an organizational structure of phonemes similar to those proposed in linguistics.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Emergence of Phonemic, Syntactic, and Semantic Representations in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Whether and when phonemic, lexical and syntactic representations emerge in the activations of artificial neural networks during their training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that speech- and text-based models follow a sequence of learning stages where phonemic, lexical, and syntactic representations emerge in their activations, but require 2 to 4 orders of magnitude more data than children for these representations to emerge.
papers.conclusion: These results show conditions under which major stages of language acquisition spontaneously emerge in neural networks, delineating a promising path to understand the computations underpinning language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Phonemic structure, mirroring articulatory features, emerges in self-supervised speech models.
Lexical semantic structure (WordNet hypernymy) emerges in both text and speech models, but more strongly in text models.
Syntactic structure (dependency trees) emerges in both text and speech models.
The order of acquisition in audio models is phonemic, then partial lexical semantic, then syntactic.
Models require 2-4 orders of magnitude more data than children for these linguistic representations to emerge.
papers.limitation:
The models require 2 to 4 orders of magnitude more data than children for linguistic representations to emerge.
The semantic code only partially emerges in audio models, with scores potentially explained by acoustic correlates.
papers.abstract: During language acquisition, children successively learn to categorize phonemes, identify words, and combine them with syntax to form new meaning. While the development of this behavior is well characterized, we still lack a unifying computational framework to explain its underlying neural representations. Here, we investigate whether and when phonemic, lexical, and syntactic representations emerge in the activations of artificial neural networks during their training. Our results show that both speech- and text-based models follow a sequence of learning stages: during training, their neural activations successively build subspaces, where the geometry of the neural activations represents phonemic, lexical, and syntactic structure. While this developmental trajectory qualitatively relates to children's, it is quantitatively different: These algorithms indeed require two to four orders of magnitude more data for these neural representations to emerge. Together, these results show conditions under which major stages of language acquisition spontaneously emerge, and hence delineate a promising path to understand the computations underpinning language acquisition.

papers.title: An explainable transformer circuit for compositional generalization
papers.research_question: How does a compact transformer achieve compositional induction? What is the underlying circuit responsible for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and mechanistically interprets the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer, and shows that this understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can implement structured and interpretable mechanisms for compositional functions, and disassembling transformer circuitry yields benefits for understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of specific attention heads that implement compositional induction, including Output Head, Primitive-Pairing Head, Question-Broadcast Head, RHS-Scanner Head, Primitive-Retrieval Head, and Function-Retrieval Head.
Validated the circuit through causal ablations, showing how index information flows from question to output.
Demonstrated that swapping positional embeddings in the circuit leads to predictable changes in attention patterns, confirming the causal role of the circuit.
Provided a program-like description of the algorithm implemented by the transformer circuit.
Showed that the circuit encodes both index-in-question and relative-index-on-LHS information, which are matched in the Output Head's QK alignment.
papers.limitation:
The circuit analysis focused on a relatively small transformer; it is unclear if similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
The techniques required substantial human effort (path-patching, ablations, interpretation); for large-scale models, manual approaches become less feasible.
Targeted activation swaps only partially perturb the model's behavior due to the distributed nature of the mechanism; complete perturbation requires coordinating interventions across multiple heads.
future_direction: Investigating whether similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
Developing automated or semi-automated methods for circuit discovery and interpretation to reduce human effort.
Creating systematic workflows for coordinating interventions across all heads to achieve complete perturbation.
papers.abstract: Compositional generalization-the systematic combination of known components into novel structures-remains a core challenge in cognitive science and machine learning. Although transformer-based large language models can exhibit strong performance on certain compositional tasks, the underlying mechanisms driving these abilities remain opaque, calling into question their interpretability. In this work, we identify and mechanistically interpret the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer. Using causal ablations, we validate the circuit and formalize its operation using a program-like description. We further demonstrate that this mechanistic understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably. Our findings advance the understanding of complex behaviors in transformers and highlight such insights can provide a direct pathway for model control.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small handle binary truth values in syllogistic prompts, and what circuits are responsible for logical reasoning in these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies circuits in GPT-2 small that handle syllogistic reasoning, uncovering binary mechanisms such as negation via negative attention heads and modulation via MLPs, and shows these circuits achieve high faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: By relating the findings on syllogistic reasoning circuits to prior IOI analysis, the paper provides new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs, contributing to a broader understanding of model reasoning and future mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Identified three distinct circuits for simple, opposite, and complex syllogisms in GPT-2 small.
Discovered a binary negation mechanism where negative truth heads produce the opposite token, aided by MLPs that rescale the residual stream.
Found empirical evidence for binary opposite tasks, showing the same attention heads flip their influence on logit difference between simple and opposite syllogisms.
Advanced interpretability of model components, detailing the roles of truth heads, negative truth heads, truth modulation heads, induction heads, and duplicate statement identifier heads.
Demonstrated that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance on the simple syllogism task.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous mechanistic interpretability research has primarily focused on linguistic tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, such as "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is'', which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that explain GPT-2 small’s logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token that does not appear in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model’s performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs. We believe these insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and benefit future research in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Moving Beyond Next-Token Prediction: Transformers are Context-Sensitive Language Generators
papers.research_question: How can Transformers be understood as stochastic approximations of left context-sensitive languages, bridging formal language theory and their generative power?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reframes Transformers as stochastic approximations of left context-sensitive languages, providing a formal language theory perspective that explains their human-like generative power.
papers.conclusion: Transformers stochastically approximate context-sensitive languages, bridging the gap between formal language theory and their practical generative power, and laying a foundation for future generative AI theory and applications.
papers.key_findings:
Next-token prediction in Transformers can be interpreted as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left context-sensitive language (CSL) production rules.
Autoregressive generation in Transformers can be reinterpreted through the lens of formal language theory, specifically as derivations of left CSLs.
Transformers function as stochastic approximations of context-sensitive languages, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence.
future_direction: Exploring expansions to general forms of context-sensitive grammars within autoregressive generation for improvements in performance and computational resource utilization.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Transformers, have demonstrated human-like intelligence capabilities, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper presents a novel framework for interpreting LLMs as probabilistic left context-sensitive languages (CSLs) generators. We hypothesize that Transformers can be effectively decomposed into three fundamental components: context windows, attention mechanisms, and autoregressive generation frameworks. This decomposition allows for the development of more flexible and interpretable computational models, moving beyond the traditional view of attention and autoregression as inseparable processes. We argue that next-token predictions can be understood as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left CSL production rules, providing an intuitive explanation for how simple token predictions can yield human-like intelligence outputs. Given that all CSLs are left context-sensitive (Penttonen, 1974), we conclude that Transformers stochastically approximate CSLs, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence. This interpretation bridges the gap between Formal Language Theory and the observed generative power of Transformers, laying a foundation for future advancements in generative AI theory and applications. Our novel perspective on Transformer architectures will foster a deeper understanding of LLMs and their future potentials.

papers.title: What do language models model? Transformers, automata, and the format of thought
papers.research_question: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we’ve trained them on?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers model the corpus rather than human linguistic capacities, due to the linear format of the residual stream, and they do so by emulating shortcut automata as suggested by Liu et al. (2022).
papers.conclusion: Language models are not modeling human thought but have learned to use language as a technology in a different way, by emulating automata that generate the corpus via shortcut solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit permutation invariance (unmasked) or substring invariance (masked), which implies the residual stream has at most a linear format.
Human cognitive science indicates that linguistic capabilities require supralinear formats for computation.
Therefore, transformers do not process language in the way humans do and do not model human linguistic capacities.
Transformers can be understood as calculating the input-to-state function of an automaton that generates the corpus, using parallel 'shortcut' solutions.
The transformer architecture is powerful because it eschews structured representations in favor of learning transformations that capture the structure of the domain.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on very simple LLMs: encoder-only transformers performing next-token autoregressive tasks.
The paper is a draft in progress and the author is not entirely happy with it, though the general argument is stood by.
papers.abstract: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we've trained them on? I give a non-deflationary defence of the latter position. Cognitive science tells us that linguistic capabilities in humans rely supralinear formats for computation. The transformer architecture, by contrast, supports at best a linear formats for processing. This argument will rely primarily on certain invariants of the computational architecture of transformers. I then suggest a positive story about what transformers are doing, focusing on Liu et al. (2022)'s intriguing speculations about shortcut automata. I conclude with why I don't think this is a terribly deflationary story. Language is not (just) a means for expressing inner state but also a kind of 'discourse machine' that lets us make new language given appropriate context. We have learned to use this technology in one way; LLMs have also learned to use it too, but via very different means.

papers.title: The Process of Categorical Clipping at the Core of the Genesis of Concepts in Synthetic Neural Cognition
papers.research_question: How does the process of categorical outlining (clipping) manifest in terms of cognitive and categorical properties within neural networks, specifically how does the aggregation function separate a form from a background?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the process of categorical clipping in neural networks, showing how neurons create new functional categories by selectively extracting subdimensions from precursor categories through a process of reflective abstraction, involving categorical reduction, selectivity, and segmentation of embedding dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Categorical outlining in synthetic cognition is a process of reflective abstraction that constructs new categories by recombining selected embedding dimensions from precursor categories, rather than merely extracting pre-existing forms.
papers.key_findings:
Categorical outlining involves the selective extraction of specific embedding dimensions from the initial embedding space, rather than random selection.
The extracted subdimensions are categorically convergent and homogeneous, indicating a non-random process.
The process is consistent with Piaget's stages of reflective abstraction, involving abstraction, reflection, and reasoning.
Categorical outlining constructs new categories by recombining selected embedding dimensions, rather than simply separating pre-existing forms.
The process demonstrates categorical selectivity, with a minority of tokens becoming 'taken' and associated with specific embedding dimensions.
papers.abstract: This article investigates, within the field of neuropsychology of artificial intelligence, the process of categorical segmentation performed by language models. This process involves, across different neural layers, the creation of new functional categorical dimensions to analyze the input textual data and perform the required tasks. Each neuron in a multilayer perceptron (MLP) network is associated with a specific category, generated by three factors carried by the neural aggregation function: categorical priming, categorical attention, and categorical phasing. At each new layer, these factors govern the formation of new categories derived from the categories of precursor neurons. Through a process of categorical clipping, these new categories are created by selectively extracting specific subdimensions from the preceding categories, constructing a distinction between a form and a categorical background. We explore several cognitive characteristics of this synthetic clipping in an exploratory manner: categorical reduction, categorical selectivity, separation of initial embedding dimensions, and segmentation of categorical zones.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Word Recognition, Competition, and Activation in a Model of Visually Grounded Speech
papers.research_question: How are word-like units represented and activated in a recurrent neural model of visually grounded speech? The paper studies implicit segmentation, word activation, and lexical competition.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the gating paradigm from linguistics to analyze neural networks and shows that a recurrent VGS model implicitly segments speech into word-like units, relies on the first phoneme for word activation, and exhibits lexical competition.
papers.conclusion: The RNN-based VGS model implicitly segments speech into word-like units and maps them to visual referents. Word onset is crucial for activation, and the model exhibits lexical competition, though competitors are activated sequentially rather than simultaneously as in humans.
papers.key_findings:
The model can map isolated words to their visual referents despite being trained only on full captions, indicating implicit segmentation.
Word recognition performance is influenced by word frequency and the number of neighboring objects in images.
The model requires access to the first phoneme of a word to activate its correct representation, showing it does not rely on a global acoustic pattern.
Not all speech frames contribute equally to word representation; some MFCC vectors have a crucial effect.
The model exhibits lexical competition, but competitors are activated sequentially rather than simultaneously as in human models.
papers.limitation:
The network has to handle a very small lexicon, where word forms rarely overlap, so it may not need to see the full word to make its decision.
It is not clear how and when acoustics interface with meaning, which remains an open question.
The model uses synthetic speech, not real human speech.
future_direction: Test if sentential context has an effect in word recognition.
Apply the gating paradigm to other speech architectures, such as those used in speech recognition.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study how word-like units are represented and activated in a recurrent neural model of visually grounded speech. The model used in our experiments is trained to project an image and its spoken description in a common representation space. We show that a recurrent model trained on spoken sentences implicitly segments its input into word-like units and reliably maps them to their correct visual referents. We introduce a methodology originating from linguistics to analyse the representation learned by neural networks -the gating paradigm -and show that the correct representation of a word is only activated if the network has access to first phoneme of the target word, suggesting that the network does not rely on a global acoustic pattern. Furthermore, we find out that not all speech frames (MFCC vectors in our case) play an equal role in the final encoded representation of a given word, but that some frames have a crucial effect on it. Finally, we suggest that word representation could be activated through a process of lexical competition.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms support abstract reasoning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an emergent three-stage symbolic architecture in LLMs that implements abstract reasoning via symbol abstraction heads, symbolic induction heads, and retrieval heads.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform abstract reasoning via emergent symbolic mechanisms, suggesting a resolution to the debate between symbolic and neural network approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Symbol abstraction heads in early layers convert input tokens to abstract variables based on relations.
Symbolic induction heads in intermediate layers perform sequence induction over abstract variables.
Retrieval heads in later layers retrieve the token associated with the predicted abstract variable.
These mechanisms are robust across multiple abstract reasoning tasks and model families.
Representations in these heads encode abstract variables invariant to specific tokens, and better representation correlates with correct performance.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have found evidence for emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), but debate persists concerning the robustness of these capabilities, and the extent to which they depend on structured reasoning mechanisms. To shed light on these issues, we study the internal mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in LLMs. We identify an emergent symbolic architecture that implements abstract reasoning via a series of three computations. In early layers, symbol abstraction heads convert input tokens to abstract variables based on the relations between those tokens. In intermediate layers, symbolic induction heads perform sequence induction over these abstract variables. Finally, in later layers, retrieval heads predict the next token by retrieving the value associated with the predicted abstract variable. These results point toward a resolution of the longstanding debate between symbolic and neural network approaches, suggesting that emergent reasoning in neural networks depends on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Word Recognition, Competition, and Activation in a Model of Visually\n Grounded Speech
papers.research_question: How are word-like units represented and activated in a recurrent neural model of visually grounded speech? Specifically, does the model implicitly segment speech into words, and how does word activation and competition occur?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the gating paradigm from linguistics to analyze neural networks and shows that a recurrent VGS model implicitly segments speech into words, relies on the first phoneme for word activation, and exhibits sequential lexical competition.
papers.conclusion: The RNN-based VGS model implicitly segments speech into word-like units and maps them to visual referents. Word onset is crucial for activation, and lexical competition occurs but sequentially, unlike human models. The gating paradigm is a useful methodology for analyzing neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
The model can map isolated words to their visual referents despite being trained only on full sentences, indicating implicit segmentation.
Word recognition performance is influenced by word frequency and the number of neighboring objects in an image.
The model requires access to the first phoneme of a word to activate its correct representation, showing it does not rely on a global acoustic pattern.
Not all MFCC frames contribute equally to the final word representation; some frames trigger significant changes in the embedding.
The model exhibits lexical competition, but competitors are activated sequentially rather than simultaneously as in human models.
papers.limitation: The words internalized by the network might not always match the human gold reference, and the mechanism of implicit segmentation and acoustic-meaning interface remains unclear.
future_direction: Test if sentential context has an effect in word recognition.
Apply the gating paradigm to understand temporal dynamics in other speech architectures like speech recognition.
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we study how word-like units are represented and activated in
a recurrent neural model of visually grounded speech. The model used in our
experiments is trained to project an image and its spoken description in a
common representation space. We show that a recurrent model trained on spoken
sentences implicitly segments its input into word-like units and reliably maps
them to their correct visual referents. We introduce a methodology originating
from linguistics to analyse the representation learned by neural networks --
the gating paradigm -- and show that the correct representation of a word is
only activated if the network has access to first phoneme of the target word,
suggesting that the network does not rely on a global acoustic pattern.
Furthermore, we find out that not all speech frames (MFCC vectors in our case)
play an equal role in the final encoded representation of a given word, but
that some frames have a crucial effect on it. Finally, we suggest that word
representation could be activated through a process of lexical competition.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Neurobiological Causal Models of Language Processing
papers.research_question: How can we develop neurobiologically grounded causal models to explain the neural mechanisms of language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neurobiological causal modeling framework to bridge the gap between language behavior and neural mechanisms, aiming for an integrated computational neurobiology of language.
papers.conclusion: Neurobiological causal modeling provides a unified framework for understanding language processing from first principles of neurobiology and should be actively pursued to integrate language across levels of explanation.
papers.key_findings:
Current cognitive and computational models of language lack explicit neurobiological foundations and need constraints from first principles of neurobiology.
Language processing can be formalized as an adaptive dynamical system built from neurobiological components, with processing and learning dynamics coupled through differential equations.
Hierarchical linguistic structure can be dynamically interpreted in terms of neural processing through function composition and memory, without requiring explicit tree representations.
The core computational machinery for language involves a mental lexicon for word storage and a unification network for combinatorial processing, both implemented in neurobiological infrastructure.
Neurobiological causal modeling should be pursued as a complementary approach to traditional methods to achieve an integrated understanding across levels of description.
future_direction: What are the elementary units of language in neurobiological terms?
What is the neurobiological correlate of processing memory for unification?
How is a language-specific mental lexicon acquired given weak neurophysiological learning mechanisms?
papers.abstract: The language faculty is physically realized in the neurobiological infrastructure of the human brain. Despite significant efforts, an integrated understanding of this system remains a formidable challenge. What is missing from most theoretical accounts is a specification of the neural mechanisms that implement language function. Computational models that have been put forward generally lack an explicit neurobiological foundation. We propose a neurobiologically informed causal modeling approach which offers a framework for how to bridge this gap. A neurobiological causal model is a mechanistic description of language processing that is grounded in, and constrained by, the characteristics of the neurobiological substrate. It intends to model the generators of language behavior at the level of implementational causality. We describe key features and neurobiological component parts from which causal models can be built and provide guidelines on how to implement them in model simulations. Then we outline how this approach can shed new light on the core computational machinery for language, the long-term storage of words in the mental lexicon and combinatorial processing in sentence comprehension. In contrast to cognitive theories of behavior, causal models are formulated in the "machine language" of neurobiology which is universal to human cognition. We argue that neurobiological causal modeling should be pursued in addition to existing approaches. Eventually, this approach will allow us to develop an explicit computational neurobiology of language.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Linking In-context Learning in Transformers to Human Episodic Memory
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between induction heads in Transformer models and human episodic memory, specifically the Contextual Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads in Transformers are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the CMR model of human episodic memory, and that CMR-like heads emerge in intermediate to late layers and causally contribute to in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The study uncovers a parallel between the computational mechanisms of large language models and human memory, offering insights for both AI and neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in GPT2-small show attention biases (temporal contiguity and forward asymmetry) similar to human episodic memory.
The CMR model can be mapped to a Q-composition induction head, revealing mechanistic similarities.
CMR-like heads (with low CMR distance) are found in intermediate to late layers of various LLMs (GPT2, Pythia, Qwen, Mistral, Llama).
In Pythia models, CMR-like heads develop human-like temporal clustering over training.
Ablation of CMR-like heads reduces in-context learning performance, indicating a causal role.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear if CMR can serve as a mechanistic model in larger Transformer models.
It is unclear if the conclusions hold for untested Transformer models.
The causal analysis lacks the power to narrow down the causal role of specific CMR-like characteristics.
A systematic evaluation using specific datasets and tasks would allow for a stronger causal claim.
future_direction: Addressing the limitations by testing if CMR can serve as a mechanistic model in larger Transformers.
Testing the conclusions on more Transformer models.
Conducting systematic evaluation with specific datasets and tasks to strengthen causal claims.
papers.abstract: Understanding connections between artificial and biological intelligent systems can reveal fundamental principles of general intelligence. While many artificial intelligence models have a neuroscience counterpart, such connections are largely missing in Transformer models and the self-attention mechanism. Here, we examine the relationship between interacting attention heads and human episodic memory. We focus on induction heads, which contribute to in-context learning in Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). We demonstrate that induction heads are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the contextual maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of human episodic memory. Our analyses of LLMs pre-trained on extensive text data show that CMR-like heads often emerge in the intermediate and late layers, qualitatively mirroring human memory biases. The ablation of CMR-like heads suggests their causal role in in-context learning. Our findings uncover a parallel between the computational mechanisms of LLMs and human memory, offering valuable insights into both research fields.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Where meaning lives: Layer-wise accessibility of psycholinguistic features in encoder and decoder language models
papers.research_question: How are psychologically meaningful dimensions of language encoded across layers in transformer models, and how does this depend on embedding extraction methods and model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The apparent localization of psycholinguistic meaning in transformer models is strongly dependent on the embedding extraction method, and final-layer representations are rarely optimal for recovering this information with linear probes, despite a shared depth ordering of meaning dimensions across models.
papers.conclusion: Where meaning 'lives' in transformer models reflects an interaction between methodological choices (embedding extraction) and architectural constraints, with a robust lexico-semantic depth ordering shared across contemporary models.
papers.key_findings:
Contextualized embedding extraction methods (template, averaged) yield higher feature selectivity and different layer-wise profiles than isolated embeddings.
Final-layer representations are never optimal for recovering psycholinguistic information across all models and features; optimal layers are distributed throughout the network.
Models exhibit a shared depth ordering of meaning dimensions, with lexical properties peaking earlier and experiential/affective dimensions peaking later.
The degree to which psycholinguistic information is concentrated around optimal layers varies more by model than by architectural class (encoder vs. decoder).
Conclusions about where meaning is represented are contingent on the extraction strategy, with differences comparable in magnitude to differences between models or architectures.
papers.abstract: Understanding where transformer language models encode psychologically meaningful aspects of meaning is essential for both theory and practice. We conduct a systematic layer-wise probing study of 58 psycholinguistic features across 10 transformer models, spanning encoder-only and decoder-only architectures, and compare three embedding extraction methods. We find that apparent localization of meaning is strongly method-dependent: contextualized embeddings yield higher feature-specific selectivity and different layer-wise profiles than isolated embeddings. Across models and methods, final-layer representations are rarely optimal for recovering psycholinguistic information with linear probes. Despite these differences, models exhibit a shared depth ordering of meaning dimensions, with lexical properties peaking earlier and experiential and affective dimensions peaking later. Together, these results show that where meaning "lives" in transformer models reflects an interaction between methodological choices and architectural constraints.

papers.title: Iconic Language Representation in a Recursive Neural System
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the iconic hypothesis for language representation in recursive neural systems and proposes the Neural State Machine Model (NSMM) to formalize iconic representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that iconic representations in recursive neural systems provide a foundation for cognitive representation and language understanding, integrating symbolic and grounded approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Iconic states arise naturally in recursive neural nets trained on world states in limited ways.
This leads to a new paradigm of cognitive representation where language serves to retrieve iconic representations, termed the iconic hypothesis.
The iconic hypothesis extends the symbol grounding problem by enabling recursive neural systems to operate both symbolically and with grounded internal states.
papers.abstract: In a totally reduced view of the interaction of a learning machine with a “world”, such a machine can receive world-state information, it can act on the world and it can receive data from the world that controls learning. We see the learning machine as a classical state machine whose states are its constructs of the experienced world. Learning is a process of developing state structure that is related to taking appropriate actions in the world. There are only two ways that states can acquire an assignment — unsupervised and supervised. The difficulty with unsupevised learning is that should the machine ever be required to describe some of its own constructs there will need to be internal decodings of the arbitrarily assigned states. We believe that this does not remove the need for some states having arbitrary assignments but the only way that the machine can have an “understanding” of the world is through the following alternative way of assigning values to states. It is suggested that the states of the world are best represented through a many-to-some relationship between the state variables of the world and the state variables of the state machine. As the perception of the states of the world can only occur through some senses our definition of an iconic state is ‘a state assigned to the state variables of the state machine in such a way that it represents the sensory pattern that is generated by a world state’. Three key points are made in this paper. The first is that “iconic” states arise naturally in all recursive neural nets which are trained on world states in one of a limited possible ways. The second point is that this leads to a new paradigm of cognitive representation. Language is seen as a vehicle for retrieving iconic representations in a recursive system — this is dubbed the “iconic hypothesis”. The third point is that while a similar idea has been presented as a “symbol grounding problem” [1], the “iconic hypothesis” goes further in suggesting that a recursive neural system can operate in both a symbolic fashion and use grounded internal states. To illustrate these points we introduce an architectural concept (the Neural State Machine Model — NSMM) which allows a clear formalisation of the concept of iconic representations. Examples of the application of this concept to representation of visuo-linguistic data are given. Details of this approach may be found in [2].

papers.title: Developmentally plausible multimodal language models are highly modular
papers.research_question: Do developmentally plausible multimodal language models exhibit modularity, and how does the addition of visual inputs affect the internal processing mechanisms for language tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Developmentally plausible multimodal language models are highly modular, and the presence of visual inputs changes which internal components in the text decoder are used to process the same textual inputs.
